bodyHtml:
What are the benefits of bringing up bilingual children?

November 29, 2017
Education | Languages

Are you thinking about raising your children with two languages? The benefits are real, but they are not always the ones people claim, so it helps to separate what research shows from what is still debated.

Here is what the evidence says about the benefits of bilingualism for children, how to start at home and why it is never too late to learn.

How does being bilingual benefit the brain?

A study published in Communications Biology in October 2024 scanned the brains of 151 people who spoke English, French or both. Researchers from McGill University, the University of Ottawa and the University of Zaragoza found stronger connectivity between brain regions in bilingual participants, and the effect was greater in those who had learned their second language younger.

The authors do not claim that every bilingual person will outperform every monolingual person on every task. The finding describes how the brain is organised, not a guaranteed advantage in exam results.

What about memory and problem-solving?

You will often read that bilingual children have better memory, focus and multitasking skills. The evidence here is mixed.

A large 2021 meta-analysis in Psychological Science, covering around 23,000 children, found that any bilingual advantage in executive function was small and variable. It was close to zero once the authors corrected for publication bias. Treat bold claims about intelligence with caution, and focus on the benefits that are well established.

The language, cultural and career advantages

The clearest benefits are the ones you would expect. A bilingual child can talk to grandparents, relatives and friends in their own language and keeps a link to a family culture.

Beyond the family, a second language gives your child:

  • The ability to read literature, watch films and follow the news in the original language
  • An easier route into learning further languages later in life
  • Greater cultural awareness and confidence in unfamiliar settings
  • The option to study, work or live abroad with less friction
  • Skills that employers value in sectors such as international trade, law, health and education

Does bilingualism delay speech?

Many parents worry that two languages will confuse their child. NHS children's services say otherwise: Cambridgeshire and Peterborough NHS guidance states that there is no evidence that bilingual children have delayed speech, and that learning two languages is a normal part of childhood.

Somerset NHS Foundation Trust explains that mixing words from both languages is typical while children work out the rules of each. If you are worried about your child's speech, talk to your health visitor or GP, and mention which languages the child hears.

Tips for bringing up bilingual children

You do not need to be a perfect speaker to pass a language on. Consistency matters more than fluency.

  • Choose a pattern that suits your family, such as one parent one language, or a minority language at home and the majority language outside it, and stick to it.
  • Offer your children several ways to hear the language, including picture books, audiobooks, songs, television and video games.
  • Do not compare your child with monolingual children. Vocabulary in each language may look smaller than a monolingual child's, because the words are shared between two languages.
  • Find local playgroups, story times, Saturday schools or community groups that use the language.
  • Give your child real reasons to use it, such as calls with relatives or trips where they can try it out.

It's never too late to start

Starting young gives children an advantage with accent and ease. The 2024 findings point to earlier learning bringing stronger connectivity, but they do not suggest older learners miss out entirely.

Classroom courses, online lessons, apps and time spent abroad all work for teenagers and adults. Motivation counts for a great deal, and it is often higher later in life.

From bilingual child to language professional

Some bilingual children grow up to become translators, interpreters or linguists. Our professional translators are native speakers who work into their mother tongue, and many have lived in more than one country.

If your business needs content in another language, explore our language services or request a free, no-obligation quote for your next project.

Frequently asked questions

What are the main benefits of raising bilingual children?

The most certain benefits are communication with family, access to another culture and easier language learning later on. Research also links early bilingualism to stronger brain connectivity. Claims about higher intelligence are less well supported.

Does speaking two languages delay a child's speech?

NHS guidance says there is no evidence that bilingual children have delayed speech. Children often mix both languages while they learn, and this is normal. Speak to your health visitor if you have concerns.

What is the best age to start raising a child bilingually?

Earlier is easier for accent and fluency, and the 2024 research found stronger connectivity in people who learned a second language younger. You can still begin at any age. Regular exposure and a clear routine matter more than the exact start date.

Which method works best for bilingual families?

There is no single best method. Common approaches include one parent one language and using the minority language at home. Pick the one you can keep up consistently.

Can bilingual skills lead to a career in translation?

Yes, but fluency alone is not enough. Professional translators need subject knowledge, strong writing skills in their target language and training in translation methods. Many also specialise in fields such as law, medicine or marketing.
